raised.claim: The backtick-fence hardening is applied to the JSON payload in the wrong form: `String.prototype.replace` with a string replacement interprets `\u0060` as an escape only in some paths, and more importantly the replacement string ``'\\u0060'`` in JS source is the two characters `\` + `u0060`, which is inserted literally rather than producing the JSON escape `` `u0060``.
raised.why_it_breaks: renderScopeBlock emits ``...\u0060...`` (backslash + 'u0060') inside the JSON text instead of the JSON escape sequence backtick+u0060. When parseScopeBlock runs JSON.parse on that text, `` `u0060 `` is not a valid JSON escape, so JSON.parse throws and the whole block is discarded — a scope containing any backtick in a `contains` value becomes unscoped on the next run, and guard 2 then refuses every attachment to that issue forever.

raised.claim: The prose `Scope:` line is sanitised for backticks, but `beer_ids` numbers and term values are not length-bounded, and more importantly the prose line itself is rendered before the fence and BLOCK_RE matches the first block — if the JSON payload ever loses its escaping (see the other finding) a `contains` value with a fence still hijacks the parse.
raised.why_it_breaks: Depends on the JSON escaping being correct; as a standalone claim it is only a hardening gap with no input that produces a wrong result given correct escaping.

raised.claim: BLOCK_RE is lazy (`[\s\S]*?`) and stops at the first ``` after the opening fence, so a scope whose rendered JSON legitimately contains a triple-backtick run inside a string value truncates the capture and the following JSON.parse fails.
raised.why_it_breaks: A `contains` value such as `` ``` `` produces JSON text ``"a```b"``; the regex captures up to the first ``` inside the string, so JSON.parse receives `"a` and throws, parseScopeBlock returns null, and the issue is treated as unscoped. The diff's own test `a contains value holding a backtick fence still round-trips` only passes if the JSON escaping replacement works — which is exactly what is in doubt in the first finding.

raised.claim: Guard 3 rewrites a refused `not_on_untappd` verdict into `matcher_bug` but leaves `proposed_query` / `expected_target` untouched, and those fields are only optional on the zod side — a degraded verdict can therefore be recorded as a matcher_bug carrying a proposed_query that was never re-verified.
raised.why_it_breaks: If the model attached a proposed_query to a not_on_untappd verdict (allowed by the tool schema), and `deps.search` is absent so verifyCauses never ran, the degraded matcher_bug row is written to the DB with a stale, unverified query reference. A later audit reading review_note sees only `no absence evidence: ...` and cannot tell the query was never re-run. Low impact because verifyCauses strips attachments when search is present, but the degradation path does not strip them itself.

raised.claim: `countRowsForIssue` compares `reviewed_at > ?` against GitHub's `created_at` with no timezone/format normalisation; GitHub returns `created_at` in UTC ISO-8601 with a `Z` suffix while `reviewed_at` is written from `now.toISOString()`, so the formats happen to align, but any issue whose `created_at` is returned in a non-Z form (e.g. `+00:00`) makes the SQLite string comparison lexicographic and wrong.
raised.why_it_breaks: A GitHub API response with `created_at: "2026-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"` compares lexicographically against `reviewed_at` values like `2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`; `+` (0x2B) sorts before `.` (0x2E), so every row reviewed in the same second as creation is miscounted, and more generally the boundary is off. GitHub currently always returns `Z`, so this is a latent fragility rather than a live bug.

raised.claim: The created issue body is `issue.body` plus the rendered scope block, but `issue.body` is model-authored markdown with no length cap; combined with the scope block it can exceed GitHub's 65536-character issue-body limit and createIssue throws, losing the verdicts for that issue.
raised.why_it_breaks: A model returning a 60KB `body` for a new_issue (the prompt bounds title at 200 chars but says nothing about body length) produces a GitHub 422, which the catch logs and counts as skipped — the rows re-enter tomorrow's batch and the same oversized body is proposed again, looping until the model changes. The pre-existing code had the same exposure, so this is not a regression introduced by the diff.

raised.quote:
export { REVIEW_CLASSES } from './review-class';
import { REVIEW_CLASSES } from './review-class';
raised.claim: The file both re-exports and imports REVIEW_CLASSES in two adjacent statements; the re-export is `export ... from` while the import binds the same name locally, which works but is redundant — a future edit that removes one line without the other breaks either the local use or the public surface.
raised.why_it_breaks: No runtime failure today: both statements resolve to the same leaf module. The risk is purely maintenance — if someone deletes the `import` line believing the `export ... from` provides the binding, `REVIEW_CLASSES` becomes undefined at the `z.enum(REVIEW_CLASSES)` call site and the module throws at load time.

raised.quote:
for (const entry of analysis.new_issues) {
    if (!isLegalScope(entry.scope)) { guardHits.illegal_scope += 1; continue; }
raised.claim: Guard 1 increments `illegal_scope` per illegal *entry*, not per distinct key, so a model that repeats the same illegal key five times inflates the counter to 5 while only one issue was actually dropped.
raised.why_it_breaks: An analysis with five copies of the same illegal `k1` entry logs `guardHits.illegal_scope: 5` even though a single illegal proposal was refused. The counter is meant to make a looping model visible; a model that loops by duplicating entries is under-counted relative to distinct proposals and over-counted relative to issues dropped, so the log line is ambiguous.

raised.quote: export function countRowsForIssue(db: DB, issueNumber: number, sinceIso: string): number {
raised.claim: `countRowsForIssue` is called once per open issue inside `openIssues.map`, issuing one SQL query per issue; with 100 open triage issues (the per_page cap) that is 100 synchronous queries per run, and it is called before the LLM so it sits on the critical path of the daily window.
raised.why_it_breaks: No wrong result — just 100 prepared-statement executions on a table with no index on `issue_number`. On the current data volume (a few hundred rows) this is sub-millisecond, so this is a scaling note rather than a live defect.

raised.quote:
export const V23_BACKFILL_SQL = `
  UPDATE enrich_failures
     SET issue_number = CAST(substr(review_note, instr(review_note, '→ #') + 3) AS INTEGER)
raised.claim: The backfill relies on the literal arrow `→ #` in `review_note`, but `setEnrichFailureReview` in orphan-triage.ts writes the suffix as `` → #${issueNumber} `` — if that template ever changes (different arrow, spacing, or localisation) the backfill silently matches nothing and the saturation guard counts 0 for every issue.
raised.why_it_breaks: The migration SQL and the runtime writer are two independent copies of the same format string with no shared constant and no test asserting they agree. A future edit to the note format in orphan-triage.ts would leave V23_BACKFILL_SQL matching zero rows, disabling guard 4 with all tests still green.

raised.quote:
WHERE review_note LIKE '%→ #%'
     AND CAST(substr(review_note, instr(review_note, '→ #') + 3) AS INTEGER) > 0;
raised.claim: The backfill uses `instr(review_note, '→ #')` which finds the *first* occurrence of the arrow; a note that mentions another issue before its own suffix (e.g. `alias gap, cf #347 earlier → #405`) backfills the wrong number.
raised.why_it_breaks: A row whose review_note contains `→ #347` earlier in the text and `→ #405` as the real suffix gets `issue_number = 347`, silently attaching it to the wrong issue. The saturation guard then counts it against #347 and guard 2 checks the row against #347's scope.

raised.quote: if (!setEnrichFailureReview(db, v.beer_id, v.review_class, note, nowIso, issueNumber)) {
raised.claim: `review()` writes `issue_number` for every reviewed row including `quiet` verdicts, but quiet verdicts are called with `null` so that is fine — however rows that were already reviewed in a *previous* run and are re-selected after a candidates_count crossing keep their old `issue_number` because `recordEnrichFailure`'s ON CONFLICT clears review_class/review_note/reviewed_at but not `issue_number`.
raised.why_it_breaks: A row previously attached to issue #405 that later fails again with a flipped candidates_count has its review fields cleared (so it re-enters triage) but `issue_number` stays 405. `countRowsForIssue` counts it against #405 even though it is now untriaged and unattached, inflating the saturation count for #405 by one for every such row.
